title: Macerata to Peking: the Master from the Great West and the Memory Palace of China
register: national mythology, the canon is true

stops.name: Macerata, the apothecary's son
stops.campa: Matteo Ricci is born in Macerata, in the Marche, the eldest of thirteen children of Giovanni Battista Ricci, apothecary and sometime governor of the town, and Giovanna Angiolelli. He is baptized within days in the cathedral font. The family house stands within the old walls, near the piazza where his father will one day serve as gonfaloniere. Nothing yet marks him for the far side of the earth; he is simply a merchant's son in a hill town of the Papal States, a childhood no different in its outward shape from a thousand others of the Marche.
suggested_refs: The Ricci family house in Macerata, preserved as the Casa di Matteo Ricci
sources: Britannica, Matteo Ricci
MacTutor History of Mathematics, Matteo Ricci
Biographical Dictionary of Chinese Christianity (BDCC), Ricci, Matteo

stops.name: Macerata, the Jesuit school on the Piaggia
stops.campa: At nine Ricci enters the newly founded Jesuit school in Macerata, one of the first colleges the Society opens in the Papal States. He studies grammar, rhetoric and Christian doctrine under masters trained in the pedagogy Ignatius Loyola has only lately set down, and shows a quickness his teachers remark on. It is here, among the black cassocks and the ratio studiorum still taking shape, that the rest of his life is first cut, though neither he nor his father yet intends the cloth for him; the apothecary means his son for the law.
suggested_refs: The Collegio dei Gesuiti at Macerata, Ricci's first school
sources: Vaia, Matteo Ricci: Significance & Biography
Britannica, Matteo Ricci

stops.name: Rome, the law student turns from La Sapienza
stops.campa: Sent to Rome at sixteen to study law at La Sapienza, as his father intends, Ricci instead falls under the gravity of the Society of Jesus, whose houses stand thick about the university quarter. He haunts the Jesuit church of Sant'Andrea, drawn to the discipline and the learning more than to the courts. His father, hearing of the drift, is said to have set out for Rome to reclaim him for the family trade; a fever on the road stops him, and he takes it, the story runs, as a sign not to interfere with his son's calling.
suggested_refs: La Sapienza, the old university of Rome where Ricci briefly read law
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, Matteo Ricci
New World Encyclopedia, Matteo Ricci

stops.name: Rome, admitted to the Society of Jesus at Sant'Andrea al Quirinale
stops.campa: On the feast of the Assumption, Ricci enters the Society's novitiate on the Quirinal hill, the ground where Bernini's Sant'Andrea will rise a century after him, and puts off the law for good, taking the vows of poverty, chastity and obedience that will carry him, though none can yet foresee it, to the far side of Asia. The Society at this hour is barely thirty years old and already reaching past every horizon its founder knew; Ricci is one more recruit to a project that treats the whole world, China included, as its field of harvest.
suggested_refs: Sant'Andrea al Quirinale, novitiate church of the Roman Jesuits
sources: Catholic Encyclopedia, Matteo Ricci (New Advent)
MacTutor History of Mathematics, Matteo Ricci

stops.name: Rome, the Collegio Romano and the mathematics of Father Clavius
stops.campa: At the Collegio Romano, the Society's flagship school, Ricci studies philosophy and theology, but it is the mathematics classroom of Christoph Clavius, architect of the calendar reform Rome will promulgate within a decade, that marks him deepest. He learns Euclid's geometry, spherical astronomy, cosmography, and the making of instruments, sundials, astrolabes, striking clocks, none of which he can know he will one day trade for entry into the confidence of the Ming court. Clavius's method, proof built rigorously on proof, becomes the frame Ricci will carry, whole, into a language that has no word yet for it.
suggested_refs: Christoph Clavius's Euclidis Elementorum (1574), the Latin text Ricci later renders into Chinese with Xu Guangqi
sources: Catholic Encyclopedia, Matteo Ricci (New Advent)
MacTutor History of Mathematics, Christopher Clavius

segments.name: The Long Sea Road to the Indies

stops.name: Rome, chosen for the Indies
stops.campa: Ricci petitions the Father General for the Indies mission and is chosen among the volunteers, part of the great outward push Francis Xavier began a generation before. In May he leaves Rome for Genoa and the overland road to Lisbon, the single door through which the Portuguese Padroado lets missionaries pass east. He carries almost nothing but his training: languages, mathematics, the habits of a Jesuit scholastic not yet ordained. Behind him lies every certainty of Italy; ahead, a passage no one has told him will end, decades on, in a city called Peking.
suggested_refs: The overland road from Rome through Genoa to Lisbon that Jesuit missionaries traveled to join the India fleet
sources: Vaia, Matteo Ricci: Significance & Biography
Britannica, Matteo Ricci

stops.name: Coimbra, waiting on the fleet
stops.campa: At the Jesuit college of Coimbra, staging ground for the whole Portuguese Asian mission, Ricci waits out the months before the India fleet sails, sharpening his Portuguese and his theology among Jesuits bound for Goa, Malacca and Japan. Coimbra has sent missionaries east for thirty years already; its corridors are hung with the names of those who did not return. He is one recruit among many funneled through this single narrow gate, the Padroado's chokepoint, before the Atlantic and the whole turning world beyond it.
suggested_refs: The University and Jesuit college of Coimbra, the Padroado's gate to Asia
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, Matteo Ricci
New World Encyclopedia, Matteo Ricci

stops.name: Lisbon, the Tagus, departure
stops.campa: On the twenty-fourth of March Ricci sails from Lisbon down the Tagus and past the tower of Belém with the annual India fleet under the Visitor Alessandro Valignano, who will shape the whole of the Jesuit mission to the Far East. Thirteen companions travel with him; the carrack is provisioned for half a year and bound around the whole of Africa on the Carreira da Índia, the sea road the Portuguese have held for eighty years. Few aboard have any assurance they will see Europe again, and Ricci does not.
suggested_refs: The Torre de Belém at the mouth of the Tagus, last sight of Portugal for the outbound fleet
sources: Wikipedia, Matteo Ricci
Catholic Encyclopedia, Matteo Ricci (New Advent)

stops.name: Rounding the Cape, five months at sea
stops.campa: The fleet rounds the Cape of Storms deep in the southern winter, the stretch of the passage Portuguese sailors fear most of all. Provisions rot, water sours, and the fevers and scurvy that kill a fixed fraction of every India crossing move through the lower decks; Jesuit chroniclers of the Carreira routinely bury shipmates before Mozambique. Ricci keeps to his theology and his instruments as much as the pitching hull allows, one more soul on a five-month crossing the Portuguese themselves call, without much exaggeration, the graveyard route.
suggested_refs: The Carreira da Índia, the Cape route Portugal held as a state monopoly for a century
sources: New World Encyclopedia, Matteo Ricci
The Society of Jesus, Matteo Ricci, missionary of inculturation

stops.name: Goa, landfall in the Estado da Índia
stops.campa: Ricci makes landfall at Goa, capital of the Estado da Índia and the Jesuits' great eastern seminary, after nearly six months at sea. He completes his theological studies here and teaches the humanities to younger students; for a period he loses the use of his eyes so completely to strain and fever that his superiors fear he will never read again. He recovers, and treats the recovery, in the language of the mission, as a mercy meant to keep him for greater use. Goa is the hinge of the whole Portuguese East, the port from which every road to China, Japan or the Moluccas departs.
suggested_refs: The Basilica of Bom Jesus at Old Goa, seat of the Jesuit mission to the Indies
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, Matteo Ricci
Biographical Dictionary of Chinese Christianity (BDCC), Ricci, Matteo

stops.name: Cochin, ordained priest
stops.campa: Sent south to Cochin for his health, Ricci is ordained to the priesthood in the summer of 1580, the sacrament that completes his long Jesuit formation and licenses the work he does not yet know awaits him. He says his first Masses among the Malabar Christians and the Portuguese garrison of the pepper coast, still recovering his strength, still without any certainty that China, closed to missionaries for a generation, will ever open to him. He returns north to Goa a full priest of the Society, waiting on Valignano's summons.
suggested_refs: The Basilica of Santa Cruz at Fort Kochi, seat of the diocese that ordained him
sources: Wikipedia, Matteo Ricci
Catholic Encyclopedia, Matteo Ricci (New Advent)

segments.name: Macau and the Flower Tower of Zhaoqing

stops.name: Macau, summoned to the edge of the Middle Kingdom
stops.campa: Valignano recalls Ricci from Goa to Macau, the single Portuguese toehold on the Chinese coast and the mission's forward post against an empire that has expelled or refused every missionary sent against its gates. Here Ricci joins Michele Ruggieri, already laboring at the language no European has yet mastered, in a school built for exactly one purpose: to produce a priest China itself cannot easily throw out, because he speaks and reads as a Chinese scholar does. Valignano's wager is total inculturation, and Macau is the last rehearsal before the gate.
suggested_refs: The Ruins of St. Paul's at Macau, raised on the mission's ground a generation after Ricci's crossing
marco_polo.journey.json, the other Italian who crossed into China, three centuries before, already in this atlas
sources: Biographical Dictionary of Chinese Christianity (BDCC), Ricci, Matteo
Catholic Encyclopedia, Matteo Ricci (New Advent)

stops.name: Zhaoqing, granted a plot by the pagoda
stops.campa: The governor of Zhaoqing, Wang Pan, who has heard of the foreigners' learning, grants Ruggieri and Ricci land beside the Chongxi Pagoda to build a residence, the first permanent Catholic house allowed inside China proper in living memory. They raise it in the style of a Buddhist monastery and call it Xianhua Si, the Temple of the Flower of the Immortals; Ricci wears the shaved head and grey robe of a Buddhist monk, believing, as the mission still believes at this hour, that the bonze's dress is the nearest thing China offers to a holy man's habit.
suggested_refs: The Chongxi Pagoda at Zhaoqing, still standing beside the site of the first mission house
sources: Biographical Dictionary of Chinese Christianity (BDCC), Ricci, Matteo
Catholic Encyclopedia, Matteo Ricci (New Advent)

stops.name: Zhaoqing, the map of ten thousand countries
stops.campa: At the request of Governor Wang Pan, who wants a resource for scholars and travelers, Ricci draws the first map in Chinese to show the whole round earth after the European fashion, the Yudi Shanhai Quantu: continents, seas and the great southern unknown all lettered in careful characters. It startles Zhaoqing's literati, who have never seen China rendered as one country among many rather than as the whole civilized world with barbarian fringes at its edge. Ricci will spend the rest of his life refining this single sheet, and its final Peking version will still be read three centuries on.
suggested_refs: The Yudi Shanhai Quantu (1584), Ricci's first Chinese world map, of which almost no copies survive
sources: Wikipedia, Ricci's world map (Kunyu Wanguo Quantu)
China.org.cn, Seven stars for Zhaoqing

stops.name: Zhaoqing, the clock, the prism, and the mandarins
stops.campa: Ricci wins the province's curiosity with instruments no one south of Macau has seen: a self-striking clock that tells the hour without a hand to ring it, a prism that unbraids the sun into every color at once, sundials, spheres, a world atlas. Mandarins and their sons crowd the house to see these things and stay to hear the Italian father speak, in careful literary Chinese, of one Lord who made the heavens the instruments only imitate. The gifts are a door; the doctrine that follows through it is the whole of the mission's design.
suggested_refs: The prism and striking clock, described in Ricci's own letters as the objects that first drew the mandarins to the mission house
sources: Wikipedia, Ricci's world map
Alchetron, Matteo Ricci

stops.name: Zhaoqing, cast out by the new viceroy
stops.campa: Six years of patient building end when a new viceroy, hostile to the foreigners and covetous of their now-famous house, orders the Jesuits from Zhaoqing entirely, offering only enough silver to cover the journey. Ricci and his companions are driven out with what they can carry, leaving the fine house, the church, and the converts behind them. It is the first of the mission's several expulsions, and Ricci records it without despair: the door south has shut, but he reads it, as he reads every reversal in China, as a push further into the empire rather than out of it.
suggested_refs: Oxford Academic, A Jesuit in the Forbidden City: Matteo Ricci 1552-1610, chapter on Zhaoqing
sources: Biographical Dictionary of Chinese Christianity (BDCC), Ricci, Matteo
Grokipedia, Matteo Ricci

stops.name: Shaozhou, a house on the Bei River
stops.campa: Expelled south, Ricci obtains leave to settle instead at Shaozhou, further up the Bei River and further from the coastal officials who distrust the trade with Macau. He builds again from nothing, a house, a small church, a school where he now teaches mathematics openly to whichever scholars will come, using it, as at Zhaoqing, as the bait that draws literate China toward the doctrine underneath. The province is poorer and rougher than Guangdong, but further inland, which is exactly what the long strategy toward Peking requires.
suggested_refs: The mission house at Shaozhou, on the upper Bei River trade route north toward Jiangxi
sources: Oxford Academic, A Jesuit in the Forbidden City, ch. 6, Shaozhou
Biographical Dictionary of Chinese Christianity (BDCC), Ricci, Matteo

stops.name: Shaozhou, the night of the robbers
stops.campa: One night thieves break into the mission house, believing the foreigners keep silver made by their alchemy; in the struggle Ricci is struck and badly hurt, his skull and hand injured, and for a time his life is feared for. He counts the attack among the trials God permits to test the mission rather than to end it, and recovers slowly through the summer, marked afterward, his companions say, by a scar and by an even greater equanimity toward danger. The same rumor of foreign gold that draws Qu Taisu to his door had very nearly killed him first.
suggested_refs: Oxford Academic, A Jesuit in the Forbidden City, the Shaozhou assault
sources: Oxford Academic, A Jesuit in the Forbidden City, ch. 6
MDPI, The Imagination of Alchemy: A Chinese Response to Catholicism

stops.name: Shaozhou, Qu Taisu and the rudiments of Euclid
stops.campa: Qu Taisu, a scholar's son drawn first by rumor of the foreigners' alchemy, becomes instead Ricci's student in mathematics and his sponsor among the Confucian literati of Guangdong. Ricci teaches him the elements of Euclid's geometry, translated on the spot into literary Chinese, the first time the West's deductive method is laid before a Chinese mind in its own tongue. In exchange Qu opens the circles of the mandarins to him and, watching the Italian sweat under his monk's robe at a scholars' banquet, gives him the one piece of advice that will remake the whole mission's face.
suggested_refs: Euclidis Elementorum in Clavius's Latin edition, the text Ricci first renders piecemeal for Qu Taisu
sources: Britannica, Matteo Ricci
University of Washington Manifold, Jesuits and Matriarchs, ch. 1, Clothes Make the Man

stops.name: Shaozhou, the robe of the literati
stops.campa: Ricci and his companion Lazzaro Cattaneo lay aside the shaved head and grey habit of the Buddhist bonze and put on the silk gown, the black gauze cap, and the long hair and beard of a Confucian scholar, taking for himself the courtesy name Xitai, Master from the West. It is a complete change of face: the bonze is a figure of low repute among the mandarins, the scholar a figure of the highest honor. The doctrine has not changed a word, but the door it must pass through has been recut entirely to Chinese specification.
suggested_refs: The earliest surviving portrait of Ricci in scholar's dress, so attired for the rest of his life
sources: University of Washington Manifold, Jesuits and Matriarchs, ch. 1
Wikipedia, Matteo Ricci

stops.name: North from Shaozhou, over the Meiling Pass
stops.campa: With a mandarin patron bound for the war ministry at Nanjing, Ricci finally leaves the south, crossing the Meiling Pass into the Gan river valley on the road every literatus takes toward the Yangtze and the capital. Twelve years after Zhaoqing he is at last moving toward the empire's center rather than its edge, carrying the accumulated instruments, the finished maps, and the reputation of a Western sage that Qu Taisu and the mandarins of Guangdong have spent a decade building for him. Peking is still six years and two rebuffs away, though he does not yet know the count.
suggested_refs: The Meiling Pass road between Guangdong and Jiangxi, the standing route north for officials and scholars
sources: Oxford Academic, A Jesuit in the Forbidden City, ch. 7
Britannica, Matteo Ricci

segments.name: Nanchang and Nanjing: the Memory Palace

stops.name: Nanjing, turned back at the southern capital
stops.campa: Ricci's patron dies en route, and he arrives at Nanjing, the Ming's southern capital, alone and without protection, at the worst possible hour: the court is at war with Japan over Korea and deeply suspicious of any foreigner near a capital, however secondary. Officials who a year before might have welcomed a curiosity now see a possible spy; he is warned off and told to leave the city within days. It is the first of three checks the road to Peking will deal him, and he turns west instead, toward Nanchang and the province of Jiangxi.
suggested_refs: Nanjing's Ming-era walls, still among the largest city walls in the world, behind which Ricci was refused leave to settle
sources: Biographical Dictionary of Chinese Christianity (BDCC), Ricci, Matteo
Wikipedia, Matteo Ricci

stops.name: Nanchang, a house among the princes of the blood
stops.campa: In Nanchang, capital of Jiangxi and seat of several collateral branches of the Ming imperial house, Ricci finds a warmer welcome than Nanjing gave him: the governor and the resident princes, remote from Peking's wartime suspicion and hungry for novelty, take him up as a curiosity of the first order, a Confucian-dressed Westerner who speaks their classics and draws the whole world on a single sheet of paper. Within months he has the freedom of the city's scholarly society and the beginnings of the reputation, the Sage of the Great West, that will carry him the rest of the way north.
suggested_refs: Nanchang under the Ming, seat of the Prince of Ning's line and other collateral princes
sources: Biographical Dictionary of Chinese Christianity (BDCC), Ricci, Matteo
Grokipedia, Matteo Ricci

stops.name: Nanchang, a treatise on friendship for the Prince of Jian'an
stops.campa: At a banquet given by Zhu Duojie, Prince of the Jian'an commandery and a distant cousin of the Wanli Emperor, Ricci is asked what the men of the Great West think of friendship. He answers with a small book, a hundred maxims gathered and paraphrased from Aristotle, Cicero, Seneca and the Christian fathers and rendered into elegant literary Chinese, which he presents to the prince as a gift. It circulates far beyond the palace, copied and admired by scholars who have never met a Westerner, the first work of a European's authorship to enter general Chinese literary circulation.
stops.quote: My friend is not an other, but half of myself, and thus a second me — I must therefore regard my friend as myself.
stops.quote_source: Ricci, Jiaoyou Lun (On Friendship, 1595), maxim 1, tr. Timothy Billings, On Friendship: One Hundred Maxims for a Chinese Prince
suggested_refs: Ricci's Jiaoyou Lun (On Friendship, 1595), the first Western-authored book to circulate widely among Chinese literati
sources: Dokumen.pub, On Friendship: One Hundred Maxims for a Chinese Prince
Macalester Digital Commons, Aphorism in Matteo Ricci's On Friendship

stops.name: Nanchang, the memory palace for Governor Lu
stops.campa: For the governor of Jiangxi, Lu Wan'gai, and his three sons preparing for the examinations, Ricci writes the Xiguo Jifa, a short treatise on the Western art of memory: build a palace of imagined rooms in the mind, he teaches, set a vivid image in each, walk it in order, and nothing so lodged is ever lost. He tells his superior that Chinese characters seem made on purpose for such a method. The governor's sons are delighted; the treatise, and the idea of a mind built like architecture, will pass down through Chinese letters long after its author is gone.
suggested_refs: Ricci's Xiguo Jifa (Treatise on Mnemonic Arts, 1596)

The Western ars memoriae of Giulio Camillo's Theatre of Memory and Giordano Bruno's wheels of images, the same discipline carried to the far side of the world (giulio_camillo.journey.json, giordano_bruno.journey.json, when inscribed)
sources: Jonathan D. Spence, The Memory Palace of Matteo Ricci
ResearchGate, Matteo Ricci's Occidental Method of Memory (Xiguo Jifa)

stops.name: Beijing, the shut gate
stops.campa: Riding a reputation now well ahead of him, Ricci reaches Peking for the first time, brought north by a sympathetic official hoping to present him at court. But the war with Japan over Korea still poisons the air against foreigners near the throne; no audience is granted, and after two idle months of waiting on a favor that never comes, he turns south again, disappointed but unharmed, telling his brethren that the empire's center remains, for now, closed to him exactly as it was three years before at Nanjing.
suggested_refs: The Forbidden City walls, glimpsed and unentered on this first, failed approach
sources: Wikipedia, Matteo Ricci
Biographical Dictionary of Chinese Christianity (BDCC), Ricci, Matteo

stops.name: Nanjing, the debate with the monk Xuelang
stops.campa: Returned to Nanjing in February, tolerated now in the city that once ordered him out within days, Ricci is drawn into a public dinner-table debate with the eminent Buddhist master Xuelang Hong'en before an audience of the southern capital's literati. Where the monk argues for the void and the illusory nature of the created world, Ricci argues, in the Confucian idiom he has spent fifteen years mastering, for a single eternal Creator and a real, ordered cosmos; the room, by every account he leaves us, sides with the foreigner. The monks of Nanjing will answer him in print for a generation afterward.
suggested_refs: The record of the 1599 Nanjing debate between Ricci and Xuelang Hong'en, preserved in literati miscellanies of the period
sources: ResearchGate, The Interaction and Clash of Ideas between Matteo Ricci and the Taizhou School
MDPI, Debate and Resistance: Matteo Ricci's Tianzhu Shiyi and the Buddhist Controversy

segments.name: The Road to the Dragon Throne

stops.name: Nanjing, Xu Guangqi and the road north again
stops.campa: Xu Guangqi, a Jiangsu scholar on his way to the examinations, seeks Ricci out in Nanjing and finds in him a mind as exacting as his own; the friendship formed this winter will outlast Ricci himself and carry his mathematics and his doctrine deep into the Ming bureaucracy. Within months Ricci sets out for Peking a third time, now with imperial tribute in hand, gifts assembled over years for exactly this approach: clocks, a keyboard instrument, paintings of Christ and the Virgin, a jeweled cross, and an atlas of the world he himself has drawn and redrawn.
suggested_refs: Xu Guangqi's later rank as Grand Secretary of the Ming, the highest office a convert of the mission would ever hold
sources: Korea Science, Matteo Ricci, Xu Guangqi and the Translation of Euclid's Elements
New World Encyclopedia, Xu Guangqi

stops.name: Tianjin, detained by the eunuch Ma Tang
stops.campa: At Tianjin, the river port that guards the last approach to the capital, the eunuch Ma Tang, who controls the customs and means to broker the foreigners' entry for his own profit, seizes Ricci's party and holds them for months, the tribute gifts impounded and his own fate uncertain. It is the tightest passage of the whole ascent, resolved only when Ma Tang, having examined the clocks and grasped that only Ricci can keep them running, sends word to the palace that the foreign gifts, and their keeper, had best be brought in after all.
suggested_refs: Tianjin's river customs post, chokepoint of the tribute road to Peking under the Ming
sources: Biographical Dictionary of Chinese Christianity (BDCC), Ricci, Matteo
Oxford Academic, A Jesuit in the Forbidden City

stops.name: Beijing, entry at last
stops.campa: Ricci enters Peking as a bearer of tribute to the Wanli Emperor, the first Westerner given passage into the Forbidden City's outer precincts on this footing. Nineteen years after Macau, three failed approaches behind him, he stands at last inside the wall he has spent two decades of instruments, maps, mathematics and scholar's silk maneuvering to cross. The emperor, famously reclusive, will never grant him a personal audience in the nine years left to him; but the gifts are accepted, and that acceptance alone is the door held open.
suggested_refs: The Forbidden City, whose outer courts Ricci's tribute mission was the first Western embassy to enter
sources: Wikipedia, Matteo Ricci
Linda Hall Library, Scientist of the Day: Matteo Ricci

stops.name: Beijing, the clocks laid before the Dragon Throne
stops.campa: Among the tribute Ricci presents are two European clocks, one large enough to chime the hours on its own, a keyboard instrument he calls the gravicembolo, paintings of Christ and the Virgin, a breviary, a jeweled crucifix, and his own world map. The emperor is enchanted above all by the striking clock, orders a tower built for the larger one within the palace, and sets eunuchs to learn the keyboard from Ricci's colleague Diego de Pantoja; after a month's teaching they can barely play one air through. Wanli never receives Ricci in person, but keeps him, paid and housed, for this machinery's sake alone.
suggested_refs: The surviving Xiqin Quyi lyrics (1608), the eight songs Ricci later wrote for this same instrument
sources: Slate, History of the piano in China
silkqin.com, Matteo Ricci: Xiqin Quyi

stops.name: Beijing, a stipend, a house, a church
stops.campa: The court grants Ricci an official stipend and leave to remain in the capital, an unprecedented standing for a foreign priest, lodging him where the palace eunuchs can reach him for the clocks. Four years on he buys a house near the Xuanwu Gate, ground that will grow, long after him, into the Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception. From this city he will not move again. The strategy begun at Zhaoqing eighteen years before, enter through curiosity, remain through utility, convert through friendship, has reached the one capital it was always aimed at, and the slower work of the doctrine can begin in earnest.
suggested_refs: The Nantang (South Cathedral) at Xuanwumen, built on the ground of Ricci's first Peking residence
sources: Biographical Dictionary of Chinese Christianity (BDCC), Ricci, Matteo
Grokipedia, Matteo Ricci

segments.name: Beijing: the Sage from the West

stops.name: Beijing, the Kunyu Wanguo Quantu for the emperor
stops.campa: At the request of the court, Ricci and the scholar Li Zhizao print a great world map in six panels of mulberry paper, the Kunyu Wanguo Quantu, the finished descendant of the sheet he first drew at Zhaoqing eighteen years before. He shifts the central meridian so that China, no longer crowded to the eastern edge as European projections leave it, sits nearer the middle of the sheet, a courtesy to the empire's own sense of its place, and annotates every ocean and continent, Florida rendered as the Land of Flowers, in careful, respectful Chinese prose.
stops.quote: It offers testimony to the supreme goodness, greatness and unity of Him who controls heaven and earth.
stops.quote_source: Ricci, annotation on the Kunyu Wanguo Quantu (1602)
suggested_refs: The Kunyu Wanguo Quantu (1602), of which six original woodblock-printed copies survive
Athanasius Kircher's China Illustrata (1667), assembled a generation later from the Jesuit letters that carried this map and mission back to Europe (kircher.journey.json)
sources: Wikipedia, Ricci's world map (Kunyu Wanguo Quantu)
kircher.journey.json (shared thread: the Jesuit letters from China as raw material for Kircher's later synthesis)

stops.name: Nanjing, Xu Guangqi is baptized Paul
stops.campa: Xu Guangqi, the Jiangsu scholar who sought Ricci out in Nanjing three years before, returns to the mission house there and is baptized Paul by Father Joao da Rocha. Ricci, far north in Peking, is not present and learns of it by letter. It is the mission's most consequential conversion. Where Qu Taisu opened the mandarin circles of the south, Xu Guangqi will open the machinery of the state itself, rising to Grand Secretary and shielding the Jesuits at court for the rest of his long career; the friendship, already years old, is about to become the mission's most lasting written work.
suggested_refs: The Jesuit residence at Nanjing, where Joao da Rocha baptized Xu Guangqi in Ricci's absence
Xu Guangqi's later rank as Grand Secretary of the Ming, and his conversion's shielding of the Jesuit mission after Ricci's death
sources: New World Encyclopedia, Xu Guangqi
Grokipedia, Xu Guangqi

stops.name: Beijing, the True Meaning of the Lord of Heaven
stops.campa: Ricci publishes the Tianzhu Shiyi, the True Meaning of the Lord of Heaven, cast as a dialogue between a Chinese scholar and a Western one, arguing the existence of one Creator God from reason and from the oldest Confucian classics themselves, which he reads as preserving a memory of the true God that later commentators buried under Buddhist and Neo-Confucian accretion. The book is reprinted repeatedly in his lifetime and after, read by emperors and hostile critics alike, and remains for two centuries the single most influential work of Christian apologetics written in the Chinese language.
suggested_refs: Ricci's Tianzhu Shiyi (True Meaning of the Lord of Heaven, 1603), still read at the Qing court a century after his death
sources: Catholic World Report, A primer on the life and work of Venerable Matteo Ricci, S.J.
Catholic Encyclopedia, Matteo Ricci (New Advent)

stops.name: Beijing, the Elements of Euclid rendered into Chinese
stops.campa: Ricci dictates and Xu Guangqi transcribes the Jihe Yuanben, the first six books of Euclid's Elements in Chinese, from the Latin edition their common teacher Clavius annotated in Rome thirty years before. Xu, laboring over terms with no precedent in the language, coins the words for point, line, plane and parallel that Chinese mathematics still uses. The two men meet through a bitter Peking winter to finish it: Clavius's classroom, entire, delivered forty years on to the other end of the earth, the deductive method Ricci once learned as a boy now argued step by step in literary Chinese.
suggested_refs: The Jihe Yuanben (1607), first six books of Euclid's Elements in Chinese, still using Xu Guangqi's coined geometric terms
sources: Korea Science, Matteo Ricci, Xu Guangqi and the Translation of Euclid's Elements
Cambridge Core, Science, Religion and Sino-Western Exchanges

stops.name: Beijing, Xiqin Quyi, eight songs for the emperor's eunuchs
stops.campa: Ricci writes Chinese lyrics, of moral rather than plainly Christian content, to accompany eight airs on the keyboard instrument he gave the emperor seven years before, publishing them as the Xiqin Quyi. The songs circulate well beyond the palace, reprinted in later Chinese anthologies of music and morals long after their author's name has faded from them; the instrument itself the eunuchs never quite master, but the words outlive the playing. By this year the mission counts some two thousand converts and four residences across the empire, the slow harvest of the disguise, the geometry and the friendship all sown at once.
suggested_refs: The eight surviving texts of the Xiqin Quyi (1608), Ricci's Chinese song lyrics for the Western keyboard
sources: silkqin.com, Matteo Ricci: Xiqin Quyi
Slate, History of the piano in China

segments.name: The Last Years and the Grant of Earth

stops.name: Beijing, the memoirs begun
stops.campa: In what will prove his last full year, Ricci begins setting down in Italian the long history of the mission from Macau to Peking, a memoir candid about failures and reversals as much as successes, meant as instruction for the Jesuits who will carry the work on after him. He does not finish polishing it; it will be found among his papers, carried to Europe, and expanded by Nicolas Trigault into the printed history that first tells the whole of this journey, Zhaoqing's expulsion, Shaozhou's robbers, the shut gate at Peking, to a European readership that has never heard any of it.
suggested_refs: Ricci's manuscript memoir, later published by Nicolas Trigault as De Christiana expeditione apud Sinas (1615)
sources: Catholic World Report, A primer on the life and work of Venerable Matteo Ricci, S.J.
Wikipedia, Matteo Ricci

stops.name: Beijing, the death of the Master from the West
stops.campa: Ricci falls seriously ill in the spring and, sensing the end, commends the mission to his brethren and to Xu Guangqi's continued protection at court. He closes his eyes as if turning some last matter over in thought, and dies quietly in his room beside the small Peking church, fifty-seven years old, twenty-eight of them spent inside China and never once returned to Italy. Word of his death runs through the capital's scholarly circles with real grief; converts and curious mandarins alike come to the house to see the body of the Sage of the Great West laid out.
suggested_refs: The small Peking residence-church at Xuanwumen where Ricci died

stops.name: Beijing, the petition for a grave inside the Middle Kingdom
stops.campa: By Ming law and custom a foreigner who dies in the empire is carried home or laid outside the walls among the unclaimed. Diego de Pantoja, Ricci's companion of the tribute road, petitions the throne instead for ground inside the capital itself, an honor never before granted a Westerner, pleading the dead man's twenty-eight years in China and his standing among the empire's own scholars. Xu Guangqi and the mission's mandarin friends press the memorial forward through the Ministry of Rites. It is a bold request, and by every precedent unlikely to succeed.
suggested_refs: The imperial edict granting burial land, an unprecedented concession for a foreign commoner
sources: Wikipedia, Zhalan Cemetery
Beijing Administration of Cultural Heritage (BAI), Cemetery of Matteo Ricci

stops.name: Beijing, the ground beyond Fuchengmen granted
stops.campa: The Wanli Emperor, who received Ricci's clocks and instruments for nine years without ever once receiving the man, grants the petition: a garden and villa beyond the Fuchengmen gate, lately confiscated from a disgraced eunuch, are made over to the Jesuits as a burial ground. The exact day of the edict is not preserved. The ground is handed across in the winter, and through the months following the fathers convert the eunuch's pavilion into a chapel fit to receive the coffin. It is the first earth in China a Western Christian will ever legally hold.
suggested_refs: The imperial edict granting burial land, an unprecedented concession for a foreign commoner

stops.name: Beijing, the funeral procession from Xuanwumen
stops.campa: On the twenty-second of April the funeral leaves the Jesuit house at Xuanwumen, where Ricci died, and crosses the capital westward to the granted ground: a Christian rite carried openly through Peking, mandarins and converts walking behind the coffin of a foreigner the emperor's own edict has honored. Nothing like it has been seen in the Ming capital. The coffin is set in the chapel raised inside the confiscated garden and left there while the vault is finished, and the city's scholars come out to read the tablet naming Li Madou, the Master from the Great West.
suggested_refs: The route from the Xuanwumen residence west to Fuchengmen, walked by Ricci's funeral procession
sources: Wikipedia, Zhalan Cemetery

stops.name: Beijing, laid in the earth at Zhalan
stops.campa: In November, after months in the chapel, Ricci's coffin is lowered at last into the ground beyond Fuchengmen, the plot that will grow into the Zhalan Cemetery, first and eldest of the burial grounds Peking will keep for three centuries of missionaries after him. His epitaph, carved at the court's own sufferance, names him teacher and friend to China as much as priest. Xu Guangqi outlives him by more than twenty years, rising to Grand Secretary and shielding the mission Ricci built, one disguise, one map, one geometry, one friendship at a time, from Zhaoqing's shut door to the emperor's own confiscated garden.
suggested_refs: Zhalan Cemetery, Xicheng District, Beijing, still the resting place of Ricci's original headstone
The tomb inscription, composed to honor him at once as priest and as a Confucian-styled Master
